strengths: First streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance with rigorous theoretical guarantees providing probabilistic bounds for CDF, quantile functions, and 1D Wasserstein estimation
Achieves sublinear space complexity O(k + log(n/k)) and near-linear time complexity compared to prior streaming OT methods (Online Sinkhorn: O(n²) time, Compressed Online Sinkhorn: super-cubic)
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse applications (point clouds, gradient flows, change point detection) consistently demonstrating improvements over random sampling baseline
Natural and well-motivated technical approach that cleverly leverages the connection between SW and quantile functions with KKL quantile sketches
Clear presentation with informative figures, complete mathematical development, and comprehensive appendix with proofs
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: theoretical results assume compact support but experiments use non-compact Gaussians; constants in convergence bounds are hidden, obscuring practical implications
Limited baseline comparisons: only random subsampling of SW is evaluated; no direct comparison to Online Sinkhorn or Compressed Online Sinkhorn despite claiming improvement

Modest practical significance: random subsampling baseline is already effective and simpler; Stream-SW remains slower than full SW when data fits in memory (Table 7); unclear when the streaming assumption is actually necessary rather than a nice-to-have
Primary novelty is in combining existing techniques (KKL sketches, 1D Wasserstein via quantiles, SW as expectation) rather than developing new theory or methodology

Incomplete experimental analysis: missing ablation studies on sketch size k sensitivity, limited exploration of k vs. L tradeoffs, unoptimized Python implementation limits scalability conclusions, high variance in some results obscures statistical significance

strengths: Novel contribution: First streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance with elegant connection to quantile sketches
Solid theoretical framework: Provides complete sequence of probabilistic bounds from streaming quantile estimation through to Stream-SW (Propositions 1-4, Theorem 1)
Comprehensive analysis: Includes theoretical guarantees, computational complexity characterization (O(k+log(n/k)) space, near-linear time), and proof of one-dimensional transport map approximation
Multiple applications demonstrated: Point cloud classification, gradient flows, and change point detection with consistent improvements over baseline
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with detailed appendices containing complete proofs and experimental details
weaknesses: Critical experimental validation gap: Only compares to random sampling baseline. No experimental comparison to Online Sinkhorn or Compressed Online Sinkhorn mentioned in introduction, making claimed advantages unverified
Theory-experiment mismatch: Theoretical guarantees assume compact support, but Section 4.1 experiments use non-compact Gaussian distributions without addressing this inconsistency

Weak experimental results: Point cloud classification (Table 2) shows marginal/tied accuracies (77.67% vs 77.67%); gradient flow improvements unclear regarding source; change point detection improvements modest on small sample size (4 subjects)

Unclear practical advantage: Paper does not convincingly demonstrate when practitioners should use Stream-SW or how it compares to simpler alternatives (e.g., batch SW on sliding windows for streaming scenarios)
Suboptimal convergence rate: Theorem 1 bound scales as min{√k, √n, √m, √L}^{-1}, and advantage over random subsampling with M≈k samples is not clearly articulated

No genuine streaming validation: Experiments do not demonstrate performance on data arriving over time with genuine memory constraints; Table 7 runtime comparisons conflate different computational models
Hidden constants: All constants C_p,R, c_p,R in theoretical bounds remain uncharacterized, limiting practical utility of guarantees
Hyperparameter selection unaddressed: No guidance on choosing sketch size k or number of projections L in practice; no sensitivity analysis provided

strengths: First streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance addressing a novel and practically motivated problem
Sound theoretical development with multiple complementary results (Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1, Theorem 1) and complete proofs
Clever exploitation of closed-form 1D Wasserstein structure combined with KKL quantile sketches
Favorable space complexity O(k + log(n/k)) logarithmic in stream size n, enabling memory-constrained applications
Comprehensive experiments across diverse applications (approximation error, point cloud classification, gradient flows, change point detection)
Clear exposition with helpful visualizations and thorough supplementary materials
Probabilistic error bounds characterizing approximation guarantees with respect to both empirical and population distances
weaknesses: Practical improvements over random subsampling baseline are modest; Stream-SW shows marginal gains in classification (Table 2) and is 30-100× slower than full SW when samples fit in memory (Table 7)
Incomplete experimental comparisons: Online Sinkhorn and Compressed Online Sinkhorn mentioned in introduction but never compared empirically, limiting assessment against main streaming alternatives

Theoretical bounds have slower convergence rate O(min{k₁, k₂, √n, √m, √L}^{-1}) than standard SW rate O(n^{-1/2}), and constants C'_{p,R} remain uncharacterized, hindering practical parameter selection
Compact support assumption (bounded diameter R) required for theoretical guarantees but not verified to hold in some experiments
Limited guidance for practitioners on choosing sketch size k; trade-offs shown empirically but not characterized theoretically
Experiments primarily use relatively small datasets (500 training samples for point cloud classification); larger-scale validation would strengthen claims
Implementation in unoptimized pure Python with acknowledged room for substantial speedup, making runtime comparisons preliminary

strengths: Novel contribution: First streaming algorithm for sliced Wasserstein distance with theoretical guarantees and memory constraints
Solid theoretical foundation with rigorous convergence analysis (Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1, Theorem 1) combining KLL sketches and optimal transport
Elegant core insight: leveraging quantile-based representation of 1D Wasserstein enables streaming approximation via quantile sketches
Efficient complexity: O(k + log(n/k)) space and near-linear time versus O(n) memory for full methods
Multiple practical applications demonstrating relevance: point cloud classification, gradient flows, change point detection
Clear presentation with helpful visualizations and logical organization
Consistent empirical demonstration that Stream-SW outperforms random subsampling baseline across various tasks
weaknesses: Limited experimental baselines: only comparing against random subsampling; missing comparisons with other streaming algorithms, reduced projections (smaller L), or alternative quantile sketch methods
Low-dimensional experiments dominate: mostly 2D Gaussians, 784D MNIST, 60D gesture data; claims about dimension-independence would be much stronger with experiments in 1000+ dimensions

Weak experimental details in key results: Table 1 shows suspiciously tight error bars for Stream-SW (e.g., 2.1 ± 0.02) versus loose ones for baselines; unclear if this reflects true algorithmic behavior or reporting issues
Unfair computational comparison: Table 7 compares GPU-based full SW against CPU-based Stream-SW implementation in pure Python without optimization, making runtime conclusions unreliable
Unspecified constants in theoretical bounds (A_{p,R}, C_{p,R}): bounds involve additive terms like (a_{p,R}/ε) whose magnitude is unknown, limiting practical utility of theoretical results
Missing practical guidance: no clear recommendations for choosing sketch size k relative to n or desired error ε

Point cloud classification results sometimes underperform baseline (e.g., Table 2: L=5, k=5 gives 61.33% for random sampling vs 68.33% for full SW), with no statistical significance testing or investigation
Change point detection evaluation limited to 4 subjects and single gesture type; wide variation in improvements across subjects (50-100 samples delay reduction) suggests results may not generalize
Compact support assumption required for theory but not always satisfied in experiments (Gaussians are unbounded); implications inadequately discussed
No code availability mentioned, hindering reproducibility; some hyperparameter choices (specific L, k values) lack justification

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: computing distribution distances from streaming data with limited memory is practically motivated for IoT/edge computing applications
Technically sound theoretical framework establishing approximation guarantees (Propositions 1-4, Corollary 1, Theorem 1) with correct use of concentration inequalities and mean value theorem
Demonstrates breadth of applications across multiple domains: synthetic distributions, point clouds, gradient flows, and change point detection
Clear presentation and organization with good intuitive explanations of why quantile sketches apply to sliced Wasserstein
Reasonable complexity analysis showing logarithmic space complexity in streaming samples
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Experiments only compare against random subsampling baseline. Missing empirical comparisons with Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn, and other compression techniques—these methods are mentioned but dismissed theoretically without validation

Limited novelty: Core contribution is a straightforward application of existing KLL quantile sketches to SW. Theoretical analysis uses standard tools (Hoeffding's inequality, mean value theorem) without novel insights
Theoretical sample complexity O(min{k,√n,√m}^{-1}) matches standard SW, making the practical advantage unclear—paper doesn't explain why sketching is superior to applying full SW to k samples

Computational efficiency overstated: Table 7 shows Stream-SW is 30× slower than full SW (10.6s vs 0.37s for n=50k), only 3.5× faster than random sampling, and authors acknowledge 'pure Python implementation' without providing optimized version

Modest practical improvements lacking statistical rigor: Table 2 shows inconsistent gains in point cloud classification; Table 1 overlapping error bars; no significance testing provided; improvements within noise for many configurations
Overstated claims of 'first streaming estimator'—paper doesn't establish fundamental difference from applying existing streaming OT methods to each projection
Restrictive compact support assumption (diameter R) in main theorems; non-compact support cases (Gaussians in experiments) not thoroughly analyzed

Limited experimental scope: Gaussians/GMMs have closed-form SW (why use them?); point cloud classification on only 500 training samples; no large-scale streaming experiments (n>>1M) to validate scalability claims; no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameter k
Incomplete related work treatment: Online Sinkhorn and Compressed Online Sinkhorn dismissed without justification or empirical evidence; unclear how Stream-SW differs fundamentally
Practical applicability unclear: For stated use case (IoT with strict memory limits), being 30× slower than full SW is problematic; no demonstration on actual resource-constrained devices

strengths: First streaming estimator for sliced Wasserstein distance with comprehensive theoretical analysis across CDF/quantile functions/1DW/Stream-SW levels
Elegant insight leveraging closed-form 1D Wasserstein representation and KLL sketches; clean conceptual contribution
Achieves superior computational complexity (near-linear time, logarithmic memory in n) compared to existing streaming OT methods (Online Sinkhorn, Compressed Online Sinkhorn)
Rigorous theoretical guarantees with explicit convergence rates and probabilistic bounds; proofs are complete and appear technically sound
Addresses practical streaming scenario: handles 2 million samples where full SW and random sampling fail (memory/computational constraints)
Well-organized presentation with clear figures, comprehensive appendices, and multiple applications (point cloud classification, gradient flows, change point detection) demonstrating versatility
Thorough empirical validation showing Stream-SW achieves lower approximation error with fewer retained samples than random sampling baseline across Gaussians, Gaussian mixtures, and MNIST
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primary contribution is combining two existing well-known techniques (KLL sketches + sliced Wasserstein); extension is relatively straightforward once quantile insight identified

Theoretical bounds not particularly tight: convergence O(min{k₁,k₂}^{-1}) shows linear not exponential dependence on sketch size; unspecified constants c'_{p,R} could be large; scaling with dimension d unclear
Compact support assumption required for bounds but restrictive; non-compact case only treated empirically (Section 4.1) without theoretical characterization

Experimental evaluation limited in scope: (1) ModelNet10 uses only 500/300 train/test samples; (2) no baselines beyond Full SW and random sampling; (3) gradient flow and change point detection use single small dataset each; (4) hyperparameter selection (k=100) not justified

Practical necessity of streaming unclear: experiments (Sections 4.1-4.3) use finite data where true values can be computed; distinction between truly streaming scenarios vs. finite subsampling not adequately explored; no real IoT/online learning demonstrations

Space complexity for multiple projections becomes O(L(k + log(n/k)) + Ld), where Ld term dominates in high dimensions—limitation not sufficiently discussed; Table 7 shows unpredictable scaling with k suggesting implementation-dependent behavior
Reproducibility gaps: no code/library release mentioned; KLL implementation not specified; random seed protocols absent; point cloud network architectures sparse

Incomplete design justification: choice of KLL over alternatives (t-digest, moments) not justified; mergeability properties mentioned but not explored; gradient computation outlined but not thoroughly evaluated
